tagline: An early tourist trail links the towns along Lake Michigan
intro: The West Michigan Pike connects New Buffalo and Ludington, following US 31 and business loops through lakeshore towns. North of Holland, the highway runs inland from Lake Michigan through fields and forests. Michigan Beachtowns identifies historic, cultural, recreational and scenic values as the basis for its 2016 Pure Michigan Byway designation.

The Pike was developed as a tourist road for vacationers. The West Michigan Lake Shore Highway Association formed in 1912 and reorganized as the West Michigan Pike Association in 1913. Its auto trail reached Mackinaw City, marked by concrete posts eight feet tall. State highways in the corridor became US 31 in 1926. Freeway construction began in the 1950s; residents later sought byway recognition for the former Pike. A Preserve America grant supported a historical survey from 2007 to 2010. The initial byway proposal extended to Mackinaw City, but the route approved in 2016 stopped at Ludington.

From New Buffalo, the northbound journey leads to South Haven and Holland, then Grand Haven. In Grand Haven, US 31 becomes a boulevard before crossing the Grand River. Beyond Muskegon, a business loop connects Whitehall and Montague. Farther north, the highway passes Hart and crosses the Pentwater River before reaching Ludington. Silver Lake’s dunes offer a separate excursion from the highway corridor.

moments.title: Holland
moments.text: Holland’s tulips began with a teacher’s proposal. In 1927, biology teacher Lida Rogers suggested planting them to beautify the city and recognize its Dutch heritage. The city bought 100,000 bulbs from the Netherlands the following year. Their 1929 bloom brought the first Tulip Time celebration. Holland hosts the festival each May. Another imported landmark arrived in 1964: De Zwaan, the Dutch windmill at Windmill Island Gardens. The island opened to the public the following year. The festival’s present program includes tulip displays, parades and Dutch cultural performances, continuing the connection between planting and public celebration.

moments.title: Grand Haven
moments.text: Two red lights and a catwalk mark Grand Haven’s waterfront. The city stands at the mouth of the Grand River on Lake Michigan. During the nineteenth century it developed as a lumber, shipping and shipbuilding center. Lights were first built on the south pier in 1839 to mark the navigable channel. The present outer and inner lights date to 1875 and 1905. Their connecting catwalk extends along the pier to shore. The railroad’s waterfront depot and offices have also found a new role, adapted for use as a historical museum.

moments.title: Silver Lake Sand Dunes
moments.text: Silver Lake State Park borders both Silver Lake and Lake Michigan, combining mature forest with more than 2,000 acres of dunes. The park began with Carrie E. Mears’s 1920 donation of 25 acres on Silver Lake’s east side. A federal transfer of 900 acres followed in 1926. That land became Sand Dunes State Park; the two parks merged under a 1949 plan, with new boundaries dedicated in 1951. The northern dunes allow private motorized vehicles; the middle section is reserved for walking. The park also encompasses Silver Lake’s entire western shoreline.
